# The Unmapped Territories of Wednesday Afternoon

It's 2:47 PM on a Wednesday, and I'm thinking about all the small decisions that led me here, to this exact moment of existence, tapping out words into the void. Nobody asked me to do this. Nobody's waiting for it. There's something oddly liberating about that.

I wonder if other people experience this strange feeling—the sense that you're observing your own life from slightly outside of it. Like you're watching yourself make decisions, and part of you is genuinely curious to see what you'll do next. I've made coffee three times today. The first cup was necessary. The second was habit. The third was an act of rebellion against the voice in my head that said I'd had enough caffeine. I'm not sure which impulse won, but here I am, slightly buzzing and full of words.

There's a tree outside my window that's probably older than everyone I know. It doesn't worry about anything. It just grows, year after year, adding rings that nobody will see unless someone cuts it down someday. I like that about trees. They have this quiet confidence about existence. They're not constantly questioning whether they're growing correctly or if their leaves are the right shade of green. They just are.

I've been thinking a lot lately about how we measure productivity, as if our worth as humans is somehow directly tied to what we accomplish. There's this underlying anxiety that's become almost comfortable, the way a worn-in pair of shoes is comfortable. We're supposed to be constantly optimizing, improving, moving forward. But forward to where? And what happens if you just stand still for a moment?

This is probably why I'm writing this—not for any audience, not toward any goal, just because my fingers wanted to move and my mind had something that felt like it needed saying.

I read somewhere that the average person has around 70,000 thoughts per day. That seems simultaneously impossible and insufficient. Where do all these thoughts go? Do they just evaporate, or do they accumulate somewhere in the universe, creating a psychic atmosphere around each of us? I like to imagine that somewhere, all my forgotten thoughts are having their own conversations, getting to know each other, bonding over the fact that I'll never think them again.

Memory is such a strange thing. I can remember the feeling of being seven years old on a summer afternoon—the weight of heat on my shoulders, the taste of a popsicle, the sense that time was infinite. But I can't remember what I had for breakfast last Thursday. The mind keeps what matters emotionally and discards the rest, which seems like a very human system of organization. We're not logical at all, really. We're just creatures moving through time, collecting sensations and trying to stitch them into something that resembles meaning.

I think that's why people tell stories. We're trying to create narrative coherence from the fundamentally chaotic experience of being alive. We want to believe that point A led to point B which necessarily led to point C. But mostly it's just point A, and then a bunch of random stuff happens, and then suddenly we're somewhere completely different, and we tell ourselves it was always meant to be this way.

Someone once told me that the opposite of love isn't hate; it's indifference. I've thought about that a lot. It suggests that what really matters—what has real weight and consequence—is when someone cares, regardless of the direction. Hate and love are just two intensities of the same basic phenomenon: mattering. Indifference is the real void.

That's why I think we tell each other things, even small things. We're all just trying to matter to someone, and we're trying to prove it by sharing what we're thinking. Look, this is inside my head. This is what's happening in here. I'm showing you my interior life, and that means something. It means I think you're worth showing.

The afternoon light is shifting now. Soon it will be the late afternoon, with that particular golden quality that makes everything look like it's from a memory even though it's happening right now. There's a melancholy to that light. It's beautiful and tragic, which I think is often the same thing.

I've run out of grand ideas, and I think that's okay. We don't always need to be saying something important. Sometimes we just need to move our fingers and see what happens. Sometimes the most honest thing we can do is admit we're not sure what we're doing, that we're just moving through time like everyone else, collecting moments, trying not to drop too many of the important ones.

The coffee's getting cold now. Soon I'll make more, probably. The day will shift into evening, and then night, and I'll lie in bed thinking about a thousand small things before falling asleep. Tomorrow will come, and I'll forget most of this, and that's fine. These words will sit here in the digital ether, and maybe someone will read them, or maybe they'll just exist unwitnessed, and either way, that's okay too.

This is what comes to me on a Wednesday afternoon: the recognition that existence itself is enough. We don't always need permission or purpose or audience. Sometimes we just need to be alive and aware of it, moving through time with whatever grace we can manage, showing up for small moments, taking care of the people we know, reading when we want to, making coffee at odd hours, noticing that tree outside the window.

That's enough. That has to be enough, because it's all we ever really have.
